nameStory: The scarlet tanager gets its name from the brilliant red plumage of breeding males, which is so vivid it seems to glow like a flame against the green forest canopy. The word 'tanager' comes from the Tupi word 'tangará,' used by indigenous peoples of South America for colorful songbirds.
description: The scarlet tanager is a robin-sized songbird that's like a living jewel of New England's forests. Breeding males are unmistakable with their fire-engine red bodies and jet-black wings and tail, while females and non-breeding males wear more subdued olive-green and yellow tones. Despite being recently reclassified into the cardinal family, these birds lack the thick, seed-cracking bills of their cardinal cousins. They're medium-sized songbirds, roughly 6-7 inches long, built for life in the forest canopy.

idTips.label: Male breeding plumage
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-red body contrasting sharply with coal-black wings and tail - this combination is unmistakable in spring and early summer

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Straight, pointed bill that's thicker than a warbler's but thinner than a cardinal's - perfectly designed for catching insects

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Olive-green above with yellowish underparts and darker wings - much more subdued than males but with the same overall body shape

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Song sounds like a robin with a sore throat - hoarse, burry phrases that carry through the forest canopy

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Undulating flight with distinctive black wing flashes in males, often seen flying between treetops rather than near the ground

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Stays high in the canopy, moving deliberately through branches while hunting insects - often heard before seen

habitat: Scarlet tanagers prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with tall canopies, especially oak, maple, and beech woodlands. You'll find them in both deep forest interiors and wooded suburbs with large trees, from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England. They favor areas with minimal understory where they can easily move through the upper branches.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive in May wearing their spectacular breeding plumage - brilliant red bodies with black wings. This is the best time to spot them as they're actively singing and establishing territories.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when males are most vocal and visible. Both sexes are busy feeding young, making them slightly easier to observe as they hunt insects.
seasonality.fall: Males molt into duller olive-yellow plumage similar to females, making identification much trickier. Most begin migrating south by late August through September.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these birds spend winter in South American rainforests from Colombia to Bolivia.

funFact: Male scarlet tanagers completely molt their brilliant red feathers twice a year, transforming from fire-engine red to olive-green and back again - it's like watching a bird change costumes for different seasons!
confusionNotes: Female and non-breeding male scarlet tanagers can be confused with female summer tanagers, but summer tanagers are larger, more yellow overall, and extremely rare in New England. The memory trick: scarlet tanagers have darker, more contrasting wing markings even when not in red plumage.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name and appearance, scarlet tanagers were recently moved from the tanager family to the cardinal family based on genetic research. This explains why their bill shape differs from both true tanagers and typical cardinals - they're evolutionary intermediates that remind us how bird classification continues to evolve with new scientific discoveries.
compareHints: Scarlet tanagers are the only Piranga tanager regularly found in New England, though summer tanagers occasionally wander north. Summer tanagers are larger, more orange-red (rather than pure scarlet) in males, and completely lack the black wings and tail that make male scarlet tanagers so distinctive.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Western Tanagers are easily distinguished from Scarlet Tanagers by their yellow (not red) bodies and prominent white wing bars.
Summer tanagers are the only all-red Piranga tanager - scarlet tanagers have black wings and tails, while western tanagers show yellow and black markings.
Hepatic tanagers are much darker red than scarlet tanagers and have pale bills versus dark bills.
